title: Should, need, get to
goal: Talk about rules, duties and freedoms at work — what you must, needn't, mustn't, usually do and should do.
bekal: you can say what you don't need to do with *behöver inte* and what you get out of with *slipper*
you can tell *får inte* (must not) from *måste inte* (don't have to)
you can talk about habits with *brukar* and give advice with *borde*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Första passet
dialogs.intro: Seven o'clock on a Tuesday morning. Dian has found a part-time job at a small café on Södermalm, and today is her very first shift. Before the doors open, her boss Maja walks her through how things work.

notes: **Du behöver inte vara nervös** — *behöva* (**beh-HÖ-vah**) means "to need". Followed by a verb it works just like a modal: no *att*, straight to the base form — *du behöver inte vara*, *behöver jag kunna*. It can also take a plain noun: *Jag behöver en paus* (I need a break). *Behöver inte* is the everyday Swedish for "don't have to".

**Idag slipper du kaffemaskinen** — *slippa* (**SLIP-pah**) is one of the most Swedish verbs there is: "to be spared from, to get out of (something unpleasant)". English has no single word for it. *Jag slipper jobba* = "I don't have to work — and I'm glad about it". It's a strong verb: *slipper, slapp, sluppit*.

**Man får inte äta bakom disken** — careful, false friend! English "must not" means "it is forbidden", but Swedish *måste inte* means "don't have to". To forbid, Swedes say **får inte** (**fohr IN-teh**): *Du får inte röka här* = you mustn't smoke here. Mixing them up can make a polite "you don't have to" sound like a strict ban — or the other way round.

**Var brukar ni äta?** — *bruka* (**BRÜ-kah**) + base form = "to usually do". English uses an adverb ("we usually eat"); Swedish uses a verb: *vi brukar äta*. In the past, *brukade* is English "used to": *Jag brukade dricka te* = I used to drink tea.

**Du borde ha mörka kläder** — *borde* (**BOO-deh**, the *rd* drops its *r*) means "should, ought to". It looks like a past tense — and historically it is (from *böra*) — but it's used for advice here and now. Add *nog* for a softer touch: *Du borde nog ta det lugnt* = you should probably take it easy.

**I alla fall** (**ee AHL-lah fahl**) — literally "in all cases" — means "at least, anyway": *Jag slipper i alla fall plugga* = at least I don't have to study. In text messages it is often shortened to *iaf*. **Ta det lugnt** = take it easy, and **Skönt!** (**hwönt**) is the Swedish sigh of relief: "Nice! / Phew!".

grammars.title: Six verbs for duty and freedom
body: All six verbs below are followed directly by the base form of another verb — never by *att*. That is the one thing they share with the modal verbs from Swedish 101 (*kan, vill, ska, måste, får*).
after: *Måste* and *borde* never change: *Igår måste jag jobba* = yesterday I had to work. The context tells you it's past.

*Får* has a third meaning worth knowing: "will have to" when there's no other choice. *Du får vänta lite* = you'll have to wait a bit. *Vi får se* = we'll see. It sounds friendly and resigned at the same time — very Swedish.

grammars.title: Must, mustn't, don't have to
body: This is where English speakers stumble most. Learn the right-hand column as fixed pairs.

head: English
Swedish
Example
rows: you don't have to (and lucky you)
Du slipper betala, det är gratis.
Du får inte betala med kort här.

after: *Behöver inte* is the safest choice for "don't have to" — *måste inte* is correct too, but less common, and some speakers (for example in Finland) hear it as a ban.
In a subordinate clause, BIFF still applies: *inte* jumps ahead of the first verb. *Maja sa att jag **inte behöver** komma på söndag.*

blocks.text: Swedish workplaces run on unwritten rules more than written ones, and the verbs in this unit are how people talk about them. Notice how gently rules are often phrased: a Swedish boss is far more likely to say *Du borde nog…* or *Det är bra om du…* than *Du måste…*.

head: You want to…
Say
English
rows: Det är **bäst att** du går hem.

blocks.title: Signs you will see
items: *Rökning förbjuden* — No smoking
*Endast personal* — Staff only
*Hundar får inte medtas* — No dogs allowed (formal *medtas* = be brought along)
*Glöm inte att ta en kölapp* — Don't forget to take a queue ticket
*Här får du parkera gratis i två timmar* — Free parking here for two hours

blocks.text: **Kölapp** is a little piece of Swedish culture: at pharmacies, banks, post offices and many shops you pull a numbered ticket from a machine and wait for your number to light up. Jumping the line is one of the few things that will make a calm Swede visibly angry.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 3
items: *Ta på dig förklädet* and *kom ihåg* are particle verbs from Unit 3: the stress falls on the particle — *ta **PÅ** dig*, *kom i**HÅG***.
Make three sentences that combine this unit's verbs with particle verbs: *Du måste ta på dig förklädet*, *Du behöver inte stänga av maskinen*, *Du borde komma ihåg schemat*.
